title: Pepper Steak with Onions
seoTitle: Pepper Steak with Onions | Firefighter Meal
shortDescription: Velveted steak strips, charred peppers, glossy soy-ginger gravy over rice
subtitle: Velveted steak strips, charred peppers, glossy soy-ginger gravy over rice
description: Round steak sliced paper-thin and velveted with baking soda and cornstarch so a budget cut eats tender, then stir-fried in smoking batches with blistered peppers and onions and glazed in a glossy soy-ginger gravy. Over steamed rice for the whole hall.

steps.title: Start the rice first
steps.instruction: Rinse the long-grain white rice in a strainer until the water runs mostly clear — surface starch is what turns hall rice gluey. Combine it in the stock pot with cold water at 1½ times the rice by volume and a pinch of salt. Bring to a boil over high heat, cover, drop to low, and simmer 18 minutes. Kill the heat and leave the lid on 10 more minutes — lifting it early vents the steam that finishes the top layer.

steps.title: Velvet the sliced steak
steps.instruction: Slice the round steak paper-thin against the grain — cutting across the fibers is half the tenderness in this dish. Toss the strips with half the soy sauce, the grated ginger, the baking soda, and 1 tbsp of the cornstarch, and rest 15–20 minutes. This is velveting: baking soda raises the meat's surface pH so it stays tender at high heat, and the cornstarch coat holds juice and grabs gravy. Skip it and a budget round cut chews like rope.

steps.title: Cut the vegetables and mix the gravy base
steps.instruction: While the meat rests, cut the green bell pepper and red bell pepper into 1-inch squares and the yellow onion into thick wedges — big pieces survive high heat with some snap left. Whisk the remaining soy sauce, the beef broth, and the remaining cornstarch in a bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Stage everything within arm's reach: once the wok is hot there is no time to hunt for a bowl.

steps.title: Sear the steak in smoking-hot batches
steps.instruction: Heat 1 tbsp neutral oil in the wok over high heat until it just starts to smoke. Stir-fry the steak in three batches in a single layer, 60–90 seconds per side, until browned at the edges — a crowded wok drops the temperature and stews the meat gray in its own juice. Thin strips blow past safe temp almost instantly; spot-check a thicker piece with an instant-read thermometer for 145°F. Move each batch to a bowl and add fresh oil between batches.

steps.title: Blister the peppers and onions
steps.instruction: Keep the wok on high. Add the peppers and onion wedges and stir-fry 4–5 minutes, tossing every 30 seconds, until the edges char and blister but the centers stay crisp-tender — fully softened peppers go army green and slump into the gravy. A little black on the edges is the wok flavor this dish is about.

steps.title: Bloom the garlic and thicken the gravy
steps.instruction: Drop to medium-high. Push the vegetables to the sides, add the minced garlic to the center, and stir 30 seconds until fragrant — garlic burns bitter fast in a hot wok. Re-whisk the gravy base (cornstarch settles) and pour it in. Simmer 1–2 minutes, stirring, until it turns glossy and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon; under-simmered cornstarch tastes chalky.

steps.title: Glaze the meat and finish off heat
steps.instruction: Return the meat and every drop of its resting juices to the wok and toss 60–90 seconds until every strip is coated and hot through. Kill the heat, then finish with the toasted sesame oil and coarse black pepper — sesame oil scorches on high heat, so it always goes in last, and the coarse pepper is what makes this pepper steak instead of plain stir-fry.

steps.title: Fluff the rice and set the line
steps.instruction: Fluff the rice with the rice paddle, cutting and folding rather than stirring so the grains stay distinct. Spread it into a hotel pan, ladle the pepper steak and gravy over the top or serve alongside, and call the crew within 5 minutes — cornstarch gravy tightens as it sits, so it eats best right off the wok.

steps.title: Hold for call interruptions
steps.instruction: If tones drop mid-cook: turn off direct heat and cover the pepper steak — hold at 140°F in a warm cabinet or 200°F oven, never below 140°F for more than 30 minutes cumulative. Log hold time on the pan with a grease pencil. If tones drop after service, cover hot food and keep sides on low heat or ice as appropriate. On return, spot-check proteins at safe internal temp before reopening the line.

steps.title: Pack down leftovers safely
steps.instruction: Cool the pepper steak and hot components in shallow hotel pans within two hours — deep pots stay in the danger zone too long. Label with date; reheat proteins to 165°F minimum before second shift. Store cold components separately so textures survive overnight.

proTips: Partially freeze the round steak 30 minutes before slicing — firm meat cuts paper-thin instead of ragged.
A splash of rice vinegar at the very end brightens a heavy soy gravy — flat usually means it needs acid, not more salt.
If the gravy tightens up on the hold, loosen it with a few spoonfuls of hot broth or water before service.
Keep a backup tray at 200°F for firefighters returning from a run — never serve picked-over pans to late crew.
Taste for salt at the end — hall palates run salty after long shifts.
Log hold times on the pan with a grease pencil when tones drop mid-service.
Spot-check proteins with an instant-read thermometer before reopening the line after a call.

Day-two move: chop it into fried rice with scrambled eggs — the gravy seasons the whole pan.
whyCrewsLikeIt: Big savory wok flavor from pantry staples, and the velveting trick turns cheap round steak tender enough to argue about. Rice stretches the protein through a second call.
mealPrepNotes: Slice the meat against the grain paper-thin. Mix the gravy base before the wok gets hot — there is no time to measure mid-stir-fry. Cook rice in a separate pot or rice cooker.
substitutions: Flank or sirloin swaps for round steak with no change — skip the baking soda if using sirloin; it is already tender.
Chicken thighs work strip for strip — stir-fry to 165°F internal and expect a lighter gravy.
No cornstarch? Use 1.5x flour whisked into the cold broth — the gravy will be more matte and needs a full 3-minute simmer to lose the raw-flour taste.
Low-sodium soy sauce keeps the gravy from going over the top once it reduces — taste before adding any salt.

adaptable.note: Use tamari (check soy-free brands separately) or coconut aminos. Use a certified gluten-free broth or bouillon.
